title: Nachiketa and the golden lid
word: reading the Isha in the original
hook: Death offers a boy gold and a long life to stop asking
carry: preya and shreya: the lovely can hide the good
tomorrow: what was a king thinking of when he died?

segments.voice: Yesterday, all that's born falls apart; the deathless doesn't: Markandeya, calm in the flood. Today, what stands between us and the truth. The Isha's answer isn't what you'd expect.
screen: `ALL THAT'S BORN FALLS APART.` · `NOW: WHAT'S IN THE WAY?`

segments.voice: A boy named Nachiketa ends up at the house of Yama, Death himself, and waits three nights at the door with no food. To make up for it, Yama grants him three wishes. The third: what happens to us after we die? Yama flinches. Ask anything else, he says. Take sons and grandsons who live a hundred years. Gold. Horses. Land. As long a life as you like. Lovely companions, with chariots and music. Nachiketa says: those last till tomorrow. Keep your horses and your songs. I'll take the answer.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `GOLD. HORSES. A HUNDRED YEARS.` → `KEEP THEM. I'LL TAKE THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: This is the Katha Upanishad, and Yama's reply is one of Hinduism's great teachings. Two things come to every person, he says: shreya, the good, and preya, the pleasant. The wise one chooses the good. You, Nachiketa, didn't take the golden chain so many sink in. Now Isha fifteen. Hiranmayena patrena satyasyapihitam mukham: by a golden vessel, the face of truth is covered. Not mud. Gold. Something lovely in the way, like Yama's gifts. Then the request: tat tvam pushann apavrinu. Pushan, sun, uncover it, so I can see. The next verse asks the sun to gather its rays, sees its loveliest form, and ends: so 'ham asmi. That one, I am. A neighbor tradition asks for a face too. In the priestly blessing in the Book of Numbers: The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. Jews still hear it as a blessing today. What the two share: a longing for a bright face that doesn't stay hidden. An honest difference: the blessing keeps two, the LORD and the people. The Isha's verse ends that one, I am, which Hindu schools read as oneness or as closest belonging. And the golden lid? Many Hindu teachers say it's mostly preya: the pleasant thing that's easy to stop at.
screen: `SHREYA: THE GOOD. PREYA: THE PLEASANT.` · `BY A GOLDEN VESSEL, TRUTH'S FACE IS COVERED.` · `NUMBERS: MAKE HIS FACE TO SHINE.` · `SO 'HAM ASMI: THAT ONE, I AM.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something softly bright nearby, a window or a lamp, never the sun. Notice the glow, then the thing the glow sits on: the frame, the shade. If you pray, ask the way the Isha asks: uncover it, so I can see. Close your eyes and let the afterglow fade on its own.
Reading the Isha in the original, verses fifteen and sixteen: hiranmayena patrena, a golden lid over the face of truth, and a request to lift it.

fork.setup: Yama offers Nachiketa gold, horses and a hundred-year life if he'll drop his question. by the Katha's teaching, what is the golden lid in that moment?
options: preya, the pleasant, standing in front of shreya, the good.
the question itself; Nachiketa should have taken the gifts.
gold as such; anything lovely is evil.
fork.reveal: the gifts aren't evil; they're lovely, and that's the trouble. preya is easy to stop at. Nachiketa chose shreya, and the Isha asks the sun to lift the lid.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: shreyas, the good, which Yama sets beside preyas, the pleasant, in the Katha Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Isha warns against greed for gold.
what it means: the face of truth is covered by something lovely, preya in front of shreya, and the verse asks Pushan to uncover it.

what a scholar hears: satyasya + apihitam join into one word; the same verses stand at Brihadaranyaka 5.15; so 'ham asmi is read as identity in Advaita and as belonging in theistic schools; Katha 1.2.1–3 gives the shreyas/preyas teaching.

same prayer, really; every tradition's blessing says exactly the same thing.
not really: the Isha's prayer is asking for gold.
chat.meaning: Numbers 6:25 and Isha 15–16 share a longing for a face that shines and isn't hidden. In the Isha, what hides it is lovely, a golden lid; and the blessing keeps God and people two, while the Isha's verse ends 'so 'ham asmi'.

tie.story: Isha 15 asks Pushan, the sun, to lift the golden lid that covers the face of truth.

Nachiketa.meaning: the boy who questions Death in the Katha Upanishad

Yama.meaning: Death, the lord of the dead

Pushan.meaning: a Vedic god of the sun's light and of paths

Numbers.meaning: a book of the Torah, home of the priestly blessing
